comments.author: Alexsky2
comments.textRawHtml:
For those interested, there was a 2009 outage of the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure that at a surface level seems like it could be a similar failure mode. At the very least, it is an interesting read on how the FAAs systems operate, since a lot of the discussion so far has been wild speculation from people with little knowledge on how the national airspace system actually operates: https://www.oig.dot.gov/library-item/29670

Of particular note is this section: Risks of FTI Outages for Existing Operational Services As of December 2009, Harris reported that there are a total of 20,982 services operating on the FTI network. While FAA has transitioned all 1,808 IP services supporting FAA flight plans to the new FTI fiber optic network, additional risks will be introduced when the Agency begins transitioning other FAA services, such as En Route Automation Modernization (ERAM) and NextGen platforms, which also require IP technology to operate. Moreover, there are 19,174 existing services that may be transitioned to the new FTI fiber optic network. According to FAA, transitioning these remaining services is important because FTI now connects older FAA systems that provide safety-critical voice and surveillance radar information by utilizing Time Division Multiplex (TDM) technology, instead of IP services.

children.textRawHtml:
The difference between TDM and packet switching is the same as between static memory allocation and dynamically allocating heap memory.

If you can afford to allocate statically the space for all the variables that your program will ever use, you will certainly increase a lot both the performance and the reliability of your program.

Alas, for many tasks this would result in a requirement for more memory than you can afford, especially today.

To use more efficiently the limited amount of memory that you have, you need to use dynamic memory allocation.

The same happens with your communication infrastructure. Using it with packet switching reduces the reliability and the performance of individual communications, but it uses the capacity much more efficiently, i.e. the aggregated throughput of all communications passing through a given infrastructure is greatly increased.

comments.author: AbbeFaria
comments.textRawHtml:
Ex-MSFT here, sharing my outdated POV based on working on a product that was using Microsoft Exchange and therefore was hooked onto the email delivery pipeline.

Note that the infra for M365, Azure etc is different. They would be running on servers hosted in MSFT DCs but have completely different CI/CD pipelines. M365 services have their own deployment pipelines and it takes on the order of weeks to deploy your changes to production.

Considering the fact that Outlook is down, clearly email doesn’t seem to be working. So email uses something called Microsoft Exchange Server, there used to be an on-premises version of this but MS stopped supporting it to run the cloud version hereby called M365. Email is one big “macro-service”, if you’re running Windows Server, look at the process called “EdgeTransport.exe” this is responsible for sending/receiving email on Windows Servers. There are probably multiple 100s of services supported by 100s of teams that are run while email is routed from sender to receiver via MSFT Exchange servers. My recollection is that even if one of these services goes down or introduces latency in the pipeline, it caused a major incident. When I was working in M365 Security in 2024, this Exchange Server pipeline was called “legacy” because it’s one big .NET Framework service. I don’t know if they upgraded to .NET core but developing on this was as HN comments say, very janky.

The reason Teams doesn’t seem to be down is that Teams services are completely different and are written using .NET Core and have their own separate release pipeline. It was much easier to interact with Teams services. I actually worked closely with the team that was responsible for ingesting Teams messages to the customer’s data store. Their code base was much more modern and easy to understand. Exchange Server not so much.

I don’t know if what I said is accurate but know that Exchange server code was like a fossil that didn’t change as much, over the ~5 years I worked on it from 2019-2024.

Story time over.

I notice you still haven't shared your own calculations.

As to your gloss of my comment, that wasn't what I meant. They would only be losing money until 02031 if they sold one trillion dollars of bonds in the near future, at 15% yield (something like 45% higher than what they're currently paying). This would be an unreasonably bad way for them to fund several years of datacenter construction. In fact, it's roughly the worst possible way. That's why I did that calculation: however bad their actual cash-flow situation is, it won't be that bad.

What they'll presumably actually do is sell those bonds (or additional shares) over the next several years, so that they're never paying interest on money they didn't yet need to borrow.

The interest on US$60 billion at ≈10.5% is only US$6.3 billion per year, which is about a third of their current revenue. Given that they're currently spending US$42 billion per year, this doesn't seem out of proportion.

I agree that nobody has any idea what the AI landscape is going to look like in five years' time. We don't even know if there will be humans.

However, Anthropic's existence as a company is kind of conditioned on explosive growth anyway. If their growth goes into single digits per year, or goes negative, they're dead even if they don't borrow money.

Anyway, I have been typing from my phone, so here is my admittedly back of napkin math. Anthropic has $450 billion in near to medium term commitments (through 2030) and another 500 billion after that through 2040 or so, most if not all of which they cannot cancel. So just in per existing commitments they owe already 110 billion+ per year for the next 4 years. I don't know if that is front loaded or back loaded, or evenly spread, but that is the average. That likely does not include all of their costs such as their 3.2 billion annual marketing spend, employee costs, and other annual costs such as their debt servicing which we will put at 6.3 billion per your math, all of which is undoubtedly going to grow. So they need at least 125-150 billion a year minimum for the next four years just to keep the lights on. That is not profit; just break even.

And there are signs that the revenue growth story might get a lot worse in the short term as competition gets more fierce and with companies becoming more discretionary on AI spending meanwhile the cost of computer continues to rise. Yeah, if their revenues were US$17 billion a year, and those grow by only 47% per year, that would only add up to US$210 billion of revenues by 02030. But it sounds like you're saying their revenue is growing by 44% per quarter, which would be 330% per year.

https://explodingtopics.com/blog/anthropic-revenue confirms: "Anthropic made $33.2 billion in revenue in the first nine months of 2026, up from $2.5 billion in the same period of 2025 (Anthropic S-1, November 2026) Anthropic’s Q3 2026 revenue was $17.0 billion, up 1,127% from $1.38 billion in Q3 2025 (Anthropic S-1, November 2026)".

It also gives quarterly revenue figures for 02025 (US$0.376B, US$0.787B, US$1.38B, US$2.04B) and for 02026 (US$4.73B, US$11.6B, US$17.0B), all sourced from their S-1/A. Those last two are where we get the 47% revenue growth per quarter, while the Q1 to Q2 growth was 145%.

So evidently I was erring by using quarterly figures not only for growth but also for revenue.

If that growth were to continue, they really would have no trouble at all in paying US$450 billion of expenses. They'd make US$37 trillion dollars between now and 02031, US$11.9 trillion of it in the last quarter of 02030.

This is unlikely to happen, but I really don't think they're about to implode.

In any case, though, I don't think they have US$450 billion of debt currently, and I don't imagine they'll pay for those commitments out of their revenue; I imagine they'll float bonds just like any other business.

comments.author: literallyanythi
comments.textRawHtml:
Scrolled down the page, saw this "Very Easy" 1 minute plane

https://www.foldableflight.com/planes/mystic

Started watching the video not planning on actually making it, saw that it is done with A4 paper and grabbed a random sheet at my desk to follow along. The pocket felt like a nice "a-ha!" moment. As someone who only knew the "naive" way to make paper airplanes from A4 paper, this is the best performing and prettiest paper airplane I've made in my life! It almost feels like it's not real how smoothly it stays straight in the air compared to all my paper airplanes in childhood.

Edit: Tried making the flapping wings AeroDactyl but it didn't work out :( wasn't aerodynamic and didn't flap its wings just went straight to the ground

Edit 2: Tried making the Jetstream (another 1 minute plane) and it came out well! Mine is INCREDIBLY asymmetrical and still flies better than any other plane I've made other than the Mystic!

Edit 3: Tried making the Advanced Elanus and I made it! But it's a little shoddy and much tougher for sure. Looks cool but it doesn't glide anywhere near as good as in the video (I guess you really need to perfect it.)

Final edit: My planes :) https://i.imgur.com/xnMdzJv.jpeg

children.author: chrismorgan
children.textRawHtml:
I’ve pulled that trick multiple times, normally successfully; some people appreciate such shenanigans.

A similar anecdote. There was once a bridge-building competition, with provided materials, and scores for it bearing different weight toy cars, for height and for length. Nowhere was it said the bridge had to bear any of the cars. Our group’s 15-metre long roll of tape bridge with four-pop-stick-A-frame supports, which scored three times as much as the next (… and we could have doubled its length), was unceremoniously disqualified for unspecified grounds, as I had expected. I pressed for a few days for the grounds (even suggesting the couple of not-unreasonable grounds I had thought of, such as that our team had schismed into two over the creative direction), but was not given them.

The unwritten rules about spirit can be applied capriciously.

I think ours was still the most popular bridge. And honestly one of the more realistic, just scaled for much smaller vehicles, a consistent 1:500 where most were an inconsistent 1:25 to 1:50. They were really good supports.
